演奏阿爾博卡雙管笛時，將附於半圓木拱的雙管旋律管、共同風帽與角喇叭視為整體，透過: To play the alboka, treat the two melody pipes fixed to the semicircular wooden arch, the common windcap and the horn bell as one whole, and blow through the horn to set the reed vibrating rather than putting the reed in the mouth. The animal-horn reed cap encloses the reed, holds the breath and allows circular breathing, so that playing can continue without a break. The fingers work the fingerholes on the melody pipes to change the pitch; the instrument is commonly used to accompany a tambourine singer. The basic order is a steady breath, circular breathing, and opening and closing the fingerholes.

阿爾博卡雙管笛擁有獨特的原始而粗獷的音色，帶有明顯的鼻腔共鳴特徵，音質略顯沙啞厚: The alboka has a distinctive raw, rugged timbre with an obvious nasal resonance, a slightly hoarse, heavy tone that is strongly national in character. Its range sits mostly in the upper middle, and it is full and carries well. The two pipes sound together, and the natural harmony they make gives a rich layering, as continuous as on the bagpipes, though rawer and more rugged. The timbre is neither as clear as the dizi nor as warm as the ocarina; it has a certain desolation. Its resonance is unusual, using the player's mouth and nasal cavity as resonators, which makes the tone at once ringing and slightly strange. This timbre suits old, folk material especially well.
阿爾博卡雙管笛是歐洲西班牙巴斯克地區的傳統單簧木管樂器，霍恩博斯特尔–薩克斯分類: The alboka is a traditional single-reed woodwind instrument of the Basque Country in Spain, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.22. It consists of a single reed and two narrow melody pipes with fingerholes, and a bell traditionally made of animal horn; an animal-horn reed cap covers the reed, the player blows through the cap to start the reed, and circular breathing keeps the sound going. Its players are called albokari, and it usually accompanies a tambourine singer, though it also appears in band scorings today.
阿爾博卡雙管笛是歐洲西班牙巴斯克地區的氣鳴樂器，屬單簧雙管笛，以動物角製簧帽與喇: The alboka is an aerophone of the Basque Country in Spain, a single-reed double pipe with a reed cap and bell of animal horn, and circular breathing lets it play without a break. Its usual use is to accompany a tambourine singer, and it is also found in modern band scorings. Of related instruments, the Gastarre pipe is used on saints' days and at Christmas, and the Serrana pipe was once a shepherd's pastime.
阿爾博卡雙管笛為巴斯克氣鳴樂器，名稱源自阿拉伯語 al-bûq（號角）。同類號角: The alboka is a Basque aerophone whose name comes from the Arabic al-bûq (horn). The kindred horn pipes go back to early Egyptian single-reed instruments, already known by 2700 BC, with images on reliefs at Saqqara, Giza and the pyramid of Queen Khentkaus of the Old Kingdom. Later the horn and the reed cap were added, and the horn was blown to start the reed. The alboka has two cane pipes, a wooden handle and horns at each end, and may come from the Moroccan double-horn pipe. It was established in Spain by the end of the thirteenth century, appearing in the Poema de Alexandre and in medieval church carving. Today it is played by Ibon Koteron, Alan Griffin and others, and has entered modern bands such as Kalakan.
